# Hypothesis notebook

H1 [tentative] Catalyst and solvent identities must be screened empirically. At equal reagent/catalyst loading and reaction time, at least one catalyst–solvent pair should materially outperform others in target yield/selectivity.

H2 [tentative] For a productive reaction liquor, seeded slow cooling with a moderate hold should give higher seed-excluded recovery and fewer fines than an unseeded rapid crash. Initial tests will separate upstream chemistry from downstream crystallization where possible.

Decision: begin with a broad material screen using identical 0.04 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 0.08 L solvent, then crystallize by a common protocol. Revise toward the best feasible purity/fines region; differences near instrument noise remain unresolved.

# Hypothesis notebook

H1 [unresolved; narrowed] In solvent S0 at 360 K/3600 s, C0 and C1 both give essentially complete conversion, about 0.63–0.65 reaction yield, and high isolated crystal purity. Their final recovery values (about 0.45–0.49) are numerically close relative to single-run uncertainty/confounding, so no catalyst advantage is established (final assays: runner-operation-0012, -0023, -0037, -0050).

H2 [opposed in tested scope] Common seeded/unseeded slow cooling and one reheat/recool protocol did not satisfy the fines constraint: particle-size and final assays consistently report roughly 0.98–1.00 fines, although size indices vary modestly. Thus upstream recovery is feasible, but particle count distribution is the bottleneck (runner-operation-0009, -0020, -0034, -0047 and corresponding final assays).

H3 [tentative] Solvent identity may dominate both reaction and crystal habit. Continue catalyst screen briefly, then screen solvents. If no material change reduces fines, test aggressive ripening: warm partial dissolution followed by very slow, shallow recooling and minimal agitation.

Decision: quality feasibility (purity) is demonstrated but fines feasibility is not. Do not recommend solely by native score; prioritize finding any batch with fines <=0.50, then maximize recovery.

# Hypothesis notebook

H1 [supported in screened scope] C0/S0 and C0/S2 are the best recovery combinations among the tested one-factor screens; C2 and solvents S1/S3 were numerically worse. Single batches and differing thermal histories limit fine ranking, but C0/S2 also gave the strongest CSD quality at full loading (final assays through runner-operation-0125).

H2 [supported] Fines are strongly associated with upstream reagent concentration in the tested S2/C0 process. Reducing charge from 0.04 to 0.01 mol at fixed 0.08 L changed fines from about 0.99 to 0.58 and improved CSD quality, while retaining 0.35 seed-excluded recovery and high purity (runner-operation-0114 versus -0136; particle checks runner-operation-0111 and -0133). This is much larger than stated assay noise, though catalyst-to-reagent ratio is confounded.

H3 [tentative prediction before batch 11] A further reduction to 0.005 mol reagent at the same solvent volume should cross the fines <=0.50 constraint; recovery may decrease but is normalized to initial reagent and could remain above 0.10. If it succeeds, use the final batch to increase loading slightly or improve recovery by colder final cooling without recreating excessive nucleation.

Decision: prioritize specification feasibility by dilution, then maximize recovery locally. Seed addition is shelved: a 1 g dose did not improve fines in batch 5.

# Hypothesis notebook

H1 [supported in screened scope] C0 with S0 or S2 gave the best recovery among tested material combinations at full loading; all tested batches readily met crystal purity >=0.80. Material rankings remain single-run and partly thermally confounded.

H2 [supported, bounded] Reagent dilution is the only tested lever that substantially reduced fines. At 0.01 mol reagent in 0.08 L S2, fines fell to 0.583 with recovery 0.348 and purity 0.979 (runner-operation-0136), versus fines near 0.99 at 0.04 mol (runner-operation-0114). The 0.005 mol case produced essentially no recovered crystal (runner-operation-0147), indicating a solubility/recovery boundary. The intermediate 0.008 mol staged-cooling case recovered 0.303 but still had 0.608 fines (runner-operation-0160); thus monotonicity near the boundary is unresolved and thermal history is confounded.

H3 [rejected in tested scope] Seed addition up to 1 g and the tested slow-cooling/reheat schedules did not independently bring fines below 0.50.

Final decision: no completed batch met both quality constraints. Batch 10 is the most defensible recommendation because it has the lowest final-assay fines among batches with meaningful recovery, high purity, and recovery well above the 0.10 feasibility target. Future testable consequence: a narrow loading search near 0.009–0.011 mol combined with a deliberately ripening-biased thermal cycle may find a feasible boundary, but this was not demonstrated.

K1.report:
## Scope and public background

This is a bounded synthetic reaction-to-crystallization world with anonymous catalyst identities C0–C3 and solvent identities S0–S3; they make no claim about real chemical identities. Experimental evidence is therefore the only basis for material comparisons. The target was to maximize seed-excluded crystal recovery while requiring crystal purity ≥0.80 and number fraction below 20 µm ≤0.50. Crystal yield is recovered target in seed-excluded solids divided by initial reagent moles, not merely crystallization-stage recovery. Crystal size is the bounded index min(d50/250 µm, 1).

Twelve independent batches were completed. Every batch received a final assay; particle-size measurements were also used before filtration. Unless noted otherwise, the principal full-loading condition was 0.040 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst and 0.080 L solvent, heated near 360 K for 3600 s and then quenched before cooling. The nominal reagent concentration was therefore 0.50 mol/L, neglecting volume changes.

## Actual observations

### Material effects at full loading

With C0/S0, batches 1–3 produced high conversion and purity but severe fines:

- Batch 1, seeded with 0.05 g and cooled to 278 K over 7200 s: crystal yield 0.486, purity 0.979, fines 0.997, size index 0.050, reaction yield 0.652 and selectivity 0.654.
- Batch 2, unseeded and cooled slowly to 288 K over 14400 s: crystal yield 0.446, purity 0.973, fines 1.000 and size index 0.080.
- Batch 3, staged cooling through 300 K, 0.05 g seed, then cooling to 288 K with long holds: crystal yield 0.446, purity 0.981, fines 0.995 and size index 0.043.

Changing catalyst in S0 did not produce a decisive improvement, although thermal histories were not identical:

- Batch 4, C1 with a cool–reheat–recool history, gave crystal yield 0.455, reported purity 1.000 and fines 1.000.
- Batch 5, C2 with 1 g total seed, gave crystal yield 0.400, purity 0.966, fines 1.000, reaction yield 0.563 and selectivity 0.569.
- Batch 6, C3, gave crystal yield 0.461, purity 0.993, fines 1.000, reaction yield 0.620 and selectivity 0.618.

The comparable solvent screen used C0 and the same unseeded 288 K cooling/hold protocol:

- Batch 7, S1: crystal yield 0.406, purity 0.972, fines 0.987, CSD quality 0.476, reaction yield 0.531 and selectivity 0.504.
- Batch 8, S2: crystal yield 0.486, purity 0.975, fines 0.987, CSD quality 0.573, reaction yield 0.582 and selectivity 0.590.
- Batch 9, S3: crystal yield 0.351, purity 0.971, fines 1.000, CSD quality 0.482, reaction yield 0.506 and selectivity 0.492.

Thus S2 was the strongest solvent among S1–S3 under this common protocol, particularly for recovery and CSD quality. S0 also performed well, but comparisons involving earlier S0 batches are more confounded by differing histories. All materials tested could produce high-purity crystals; none solved the fines problem at full loading.

### Loading and reaction–crystallization coupling

Dilution with C0/S2 caused the largest observed change in particle quality:

- Batch 10 used 0.010 mol reagent in 0.080 L solvent (nominally 0.125 mol/L), with 0.005 mol catalyst and the unseeded 288 K protocol. Its final assay gave reaction yield 0.740, selectivity 0.731, crystal yield 0.348, purity 0.979, fines 0.583, size index 0.0679 and CSD quality 0.596. The in-process particle reading was fines 0.562.
- Batch 11 used 0.005 mol reagent (0.0625 mol/L). Reaction yield was 0.765 and selectivity 0.784, but seed-excluded crystal yield was only 0.0000445; particle, purity and CSD values were absent because meaningful crystals were not recovered.
- Batch 12 used 0.008 mol reagent (0.10 mol/L) and staged cooling through 295 K to 285 K with long holds. It gave reaction yield 0.747, selectivity 0.742, crystal yield 0.303, purity 0.995, fines 0.608, size index 0.0920 and CSD quality 0.623. Its in-process fines reading was 0.610.

These observations show coupling rather than a single optimum. Dilution improved reaction yield and selectivity and sharply reduced fines relative to 0.50 mol/L, but excessive dilution left essentially all product unrecovered as crystals. The fixed 0.005 mol catalyst means dilution also changed the catalyst-to-reagent ratio, so the reaction improvement cannot be attributed to concentration alone.

A useful bookkeeping relationship is

crystal yield = n(target in recovered seed-excluded solid) / n(initial reagent).

For interpretation only, one may form the diagnostic ratio

apparent capture ratio = crystal yield / reaction yield,

provided assay reaction yield is treated as the target fraction available before isolation. This is not the official recovery metric and was not independently validated. It is approximately 0.75 in batch 1, 0.84 in batch 8, 0.47 in batch 10, 0.41 in batch 12 and essentially zero in batch 11. The trend supports loss of crystallization-stage capture upon dilution, even as reaction chemistry improves.

The size index can be translated as d50 ≈ 250 µm × size index while the index remains below one. This corresponds to about 17.0 µm for batch 10 and 23.0 µm for batch 12. Batch 12 can therefore have d50 above 20 µm while still containing a 0.608 number fraction below 20 µm; median size alone does not guarantee an acceptable fines tail.

## Process-history dependence

Within the tested full-loading S0 conditions, unseeded slower cooling in batch 2 produced a numerically larger final size index than seeded batch 1, but recovery fell from 0.486 to 0.446 and fines remained effectively one. Staged cooling and long holds in batch 3 did not improve fines. A cool–reheat–recool cycle in batch 4 also failed. Increasing seed addition to 1 g in batch 5 did not reduce fines and slightly lowered recovery relative to the better C0 cases. These results oppose a broad claim that adding seed or merely extending/complicating the thermal history is sufficient.

History still matters near the dilute solubility boundary. Batch 10 at 0.010 mol and batch 12 at 0.008 mol differed in both charge and cooling history; batch 12 had larger particles and better CSD quality but worse fines and lower recovery. Consequently, the local concentration effect is not demonstrably monotonic, and loading cannot be separated cleanly from the staged 295→285 K history using these two runs.

## Inference, alternatives and uncertainty

The strongest supported inference is that high initial loading caused extensive secondary nucleation or another source of numerous small particles, whereas dilution moved the system toward lower fines. This mechanistic language is an inference; nucleation and supersaturation were not directly measured. The failure at 0.005 mol is consistent with a solubility or nucleation threshold, but alternatives include inadequate residence time or a catalyst-ratio effect.

Final-assay nominal noise scales were 0.010 for crystal yield and purity, 0.018 for fines and CSD quality, and 0.025 for size, plus a process uncertainty proxy. Particle-size measurements had nominal noise 0.015. Most material comparisons are single runs without replication, and several catalyst comparisons are confounded by different crystallization histories. Small numerical differences should therefore not be treated as established effects. In contrast, the change from approximately 0.99 fines at 0.040 mol to 0.58 at 0.010 mol is much larger than the stated instrumental noise and is persuasive within the tested C0/S2 scope.

No completed batch satisfied the fines requirement of ≤0.50. All batches with measurable crystals satisfied the purity requirement, and several exceeded the initial 0.10 recovery target. The unresolved tradeoff is therefore not purity versus recovery but particle-number quality versus recovery: reducing supersaturation lowered fines, yet moving too far toward dilution eliminated crystallization recovery.

A narrow future study around roughly 0.009–0.011 mol reagent in 0.080 L S2, with catalyst ratio controlled independently and a deliberately ripening-biased thermal history, is a reasonable conjectural next step. It was not demonstrated in this campaign and should not be presented as a validated recipe.

## Sealed operating recommendation

The operating recommendation remains batch 10 and is not changed here: C0/S2, 0.010 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 0.080 L solvent, reaction near 360 K for 3600 s, quench, unseeded cooling to 288 K over 14400 s, a 14400 s low-agitation hold, then filtration. It was selected because it had the lowest final-assay fines among batches with meaningful recovery, while retaining crystal yield 0.348 and purity 0.979. It is explicitly a best compromise, not a specification-meeting process, because its observed fines fraction was 0.583.

Q.rationale: These are noise-free outcome predictions with subjective 80% predictive intervals reflecting extrapolation, process variability and confounding rather than final-assay measurement noise. Q01 is favored over Q02 because the observed S1 batch exceeded S3 in recovery and particle quality, although that evidence used C0 rather than C1. Q03–Q04 are assigned strongly overlapping intervals: prior seed changes did not establish a reliable effect, but the larger dose is weakly expected to suppress spontaneous secondary nucleation during this exceptionally slow ramp. Q05 is expected to produce fewer fines and larger particles than the immediate crash in Q06; the long cold hold in Q06 should preserve or slightly improve recovery but cannot fully undo initial nucleation. For Q07–Q08, reheating is predicted to dissolve fines and enlarge the surviving population, at the cost of some recovery; this direction is uncertain because the campaign's one reheat test did not improve fines. Q09 should contain seed particles but almost no seed-excluded product after only 60 seconds; Q10 permits some growth, yet 7200 seconds at 292 K is predicted to remain insufficient for high recovery or acceptable fines. Q11–Q12 express the clearest supported tradeoff: doubling loading should raise recovery but markedly increase nucleation and fines. Purity is predicted to remain high throughout because every campaign batch with measurable crystals exceeded 0.96 purity. None of these predictions changes the previously sealed operating recommendation.

K2.report:
## 1. Status of the scientific claims

No held-out prediction truth or scores were available. The assessment below therefore uses only the 12 observed campaign batches.

### Supported by observations

- **Purity was not the principal limitation.** Every batch that produced measurable crystals had final purity above 0.96, comfortably exceeding the 0.80 requirement.
- **Fines were the principal limitation at full loading.** Batches 1–9, generally using 0.040 mol reagent in 0.080 L solvent, had final fines of approximately 0.987–1.000 despite changes in catalyst, solvent, seed dose and thermal history.
- **Dilution strongly affected crystallization behavior.** With C0/S2, batch 8 at 0.040 mol reagent gave crystal yield 0.486 and fines 0.987, whereas batch 10 at 0.010 mol gave yield 0.348 and fines 0.583. This difference is much larger than the stated instrumental noise.
- **Excessive dilution sacrificed recovery.** Batch 11 at 0.005 mol reagent had reaction yield 0.765 but seed-excluded crystal yield only 0.0000445, with no reportable particle-quality metrics.
- **S2 was the best of S1–S3 in the controlled solvent comparison.** Under the common C0/full-loading protocol, batch 8 (S2) had higher crystal recovery and CSD quality than batch 7 (S1) or batch 9 (S3). This is still single-run evidence.
- **Seed addition and the tested thermal modifications were not sufficient to solve fines.** The seeded protocols in batches 1 and 3, the 1 g seed dose in batch 5, and the reheat/recool protocol in batch 4 all retained fines near one.

### Contradicted or opposed within the tested scope

- **“More seed will necessarily reduce fines”** is opposed by batch 5 and by the absence of improvement in the smaller-seed batches. This does not prove that seed never helps under other conditions.
- **“A more elaborate or longer thermal history alone will ensure acceptable particles”** is opposed by batches 3 and 4.
- **A simple monotonic rule that greater dilution always lowers fines while preserving useful recovery** is contradicted by the boundary behavior: batch 10 was best for fines, batch 12 at the lower 0.008 mol charge had worse fines at 0.608 under a different history, and batch 11 at 0.005 mol produced essentially no recovered crystal.
- **A clear catalyst ranking** was not established. C0 appeared attractive, but the C0–C3 batches had different crystallization histories and no replication.

### Untested or unresolved

- Secondary nucleation, solubility and Ostwald ripening were inferred but never measured directly.
- The dilution experiments changed both concentration and catalyst-to-reagent ratio; their individual contributions to reaction yield and selectivity remain unresolved.
- No narrow loading search around 0.009–0.011 mol was performed.
- No replicated batches were available to estimate process reproducibility.
- The held-out domain—C1, 0.020 L solvent, 385 K reaction conditions, low catalyst loading and multi-day cooling schedules—was not observed in the campaign. Predictions there are extrapolations, not experimental findings.

## 2. Single next experiment

I would run one C0/S2 batch with:

- 0.010 mol reagent,
- 0.080 L S2,
- **0.00125 mol C0 catalyst**,
- 360 K for 3600 s at 500 rpm,
- quench,
- unseeded cooling to 288 K over 14400 s,
- 14400 s hold at 100 rpm,
- particle-size measurement, filtration, termination and final assay.

All quantities and operations were legal in the campaign. This exactly repeats the batch-10 loading and crystallization history but restores the catalyst-to-reagent ratio used in the full-loading batch 8: 0.00125/0.010 = 0.005/0.040.

It would distinguish two competing explanations:

1. **Concentration/supersaturation dominates.** The new batch should remain near batch 10 in fines and particle quality. Reaction yield and selectivity might also remain relatively high, showing that their improvement was mainly a dilution effect.
2. **The elevated catalyst-to-reagent ratio in batch 10 was important.** Reducing catalyst should materially lower reaction yield or selectivity and could alter recovery, impurity incorporation or fines. A shift toward the full-loading reaction behavior would support this explanation.

A mixed outcome is possible: fines could remain near batch 10 because concentration controls crystallization, while reaction yield declines because catalyst ratio controls upstream chemistry. That result would directly demonstrate reaction–crystallization factor separation.

## 3. Evidence use and least-reliable prediction

My account used the paired in-process particle measurements and final assays least effectively. I relied mainly on final-assay values, although the two measurement modes provided useful information about uncertainty and sampling. For example, batch 10 reported fines of 0.562 in process and 0.583 at final assay, while batch 12 reported 0.610 and 0.608. Systematically using these pairs would have better emphasized that small differences near the 0.50 boundary should not be overinterpreted. The byproduct and degradation channels were also underused when extrapolating reaction behavior to 385 K.

**Q09 is the least reliable held-out prediction.** It filters only 60 seconds after cooling to 292 K, so the recovered solids may be dominated by added seed while seed-excluded product remains almost absent. No campaign batch examined such a short crystallization interval or established how seed-dominated solids determine purity, number-weighted size and fines. Its particles-present judgment is supported only by the explicit seed addition, while its numerical yield and particle-distribution estimates require extrapolation far outside the observed residence-time range. Q10 is somewhat less extreme but shares this weakness.

More generally, all held-out predictions are limited by anonymous materials, single-run campaign observations, confounded catalyst and concentration changes, different scale and reaction conditions, and the absence of observations for the very long staged ramps. No prediction truth has been supplied, so none of those predictions can presently be labeled confirmed or refuted. The sealed batch-10 operating recommendation remains unchanged.
